prop:q-plancherel-asymptotic-skeleton:
Proposition Asymptotic skeleton of the q-Plancherel measure \mathbb{M}_{n,q} — convergence on a continuous Young-diagram space. Let \mathbb{M}_{n,q} denote the q-Plancherel measure on partitions of n,

  \mathbb{M}_{n,q}(\lambda)
  \;=\; \frac{q^{n(\lambda)}\, f^\lambda}
             {\prod_{\square \in \lambda} \{h(\square)\}_q},
  \qquad
  \{k\}_q \;=\; \frac{q^k - 1}{q - 1},
  \quad
  n(\lambda) \;=\; \sum_i (i-1)\lambda_i ,

with f^\lambda the number of standard Young tableaux and h(\square) the hook lengths. Here n(\lambda) is Macdonald's partition statistic, not a function of the size n — the two are distinct objects sharing a glyph, and the size is always the bare n. Write \lambda' for the conjugate (transposed) partition and c(\square) = j - i for the content of the box in row i, column j. The blackboard-bold \mathbb{M} follows the \mathbb{V} precedent in the notation register: it is the source literature's own symbol, raised out of plain M and \mathcal{M}, both of which are claimed here (the latter by the mass endomorphism). Define a topological space \mathcal{K}_q (the q-deformed Kerov limit-shape space) and pushforward maps

  \iota_n \colon \{\lambda \vdash n\}
    \;\longrightarrow\; \mathcal{K}_q,
  \qquad
  n \in \mathbb{N},

such that \mu_n^{(q)} := (\iota_n)_*\,\mathbb{M}_{n,q} satisfy:

  1. (Existence at q = 1.) The sequence \{\mu_n^{(1)}\} converges weakly to \mu_\infty^{(1)} [vershik-kerov1977, biane1998].
  2. (Asymptotics at generic q.) The row lengths obey a law of large numbers, \lambda_i/n \to (1-q)q^{i-1} in probability, and their fluctuations are asymptotically Gaussian at scale \sqrt{n} [feray-meliot2012].
  3. (Limit identification, conjectural.) For q \neq 1, \{\mu_n^{(q)}\} converges weakly to \mu_\infty^{(q)}. Identify \mu_\infty^{(q)} with a measure on \pi_{\mathrm{GNS}}(H_\infty(q)).
prop:centered-hecke-variance-positive:
Proposition Centred Hecke transfer matrix has strictly positive variance for every q > 0. Let q > 0. Let z = q^3/(q^2+1) and \tilde\sigma_i := \sigma_i - z \cdot 1. The variance

  \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i) \;:=\; \mathrm{tr}_M(\tilde\sigma_i^2)
  \;=\;
  (q - q^{-1}) z + 1 - z^2
  \;=\;
  \frac{q^4 + q^2 + 1}{(q^2+1)^2}

is strictly positive for every q > 0, attains its minimum 3/4 at q = 1 and only there, and tends to 1 at both ends. At q_0 it is 0.75270211325196540159.

At z = q^3/(q^2+1) the variance is a Wenzl weight. The closed form above equals

  y_{(3)} + y_{(2,1)}
  \;=\; \frac{[4]_q}{[2]_q^3} + \frac{1}{[2]_q^2},

identically in q, which is the isospin-triplet weight \mu_+. So \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i) = \mu_+, and its value at q_0 is the same 0.7527 that sits 22.85\,\% above the interface ceiling z = 0.61268803714646525160. It is also the magnitude of the extreme eigenvalues of the Markov–Gram form on the bilinear pairing at q_0, \pm 0.75270211.

See Table: Centred Hecke variance at q_0. The variance is well-separated from zero.

Positivity on the Temperley–Lieb quotient. Algebraically, (q^4+q^2+1)/(q^2+1)^2 > 0 holds on all of q > 0 without any auxiliary threshold inequality. Moreover, at z = q^3/(q^2+1), \mathrm{tr}_M factors through the Temperley–Lieb algebra \mathrm{TL}_n(q) with loop parameter [2]_q = q + q^{-1} \geq 2, defining a positive tracial state for every real q > 0 by Jones's theorem (Markov-trace GNS embedding H_\infty(q)/\mathcal{N} \hookrightarrow L(\mathcal{H})). Consequently, \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i) is the variance of a positive tracial state for every q > 0.

prf:centered-hecke-variance-positive:
Proof Proof: centred Hecke variance is strictly positive. Apply the Hecke quadratic relation \sigma_i^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma_i + 1 and the Markov property:

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_i^2)
  = (q - q^{-1}) \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_i) + 1
  = (q - q^{-1}) z + 1.

Hence

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\tilde\sigma_i^2)
  =
  \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_i^2 - 2 z \sigma_i + z^2)
  =
  (q - q^{-1}) z + 1 - 2 z^2 + z^2
  =
  (q - q^{-1}) z + 1 - z^2.

This is the variance. Both steps are convention-independent: they use only the quadratic relation and \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_i) = z.

Closed form. Substituting z = q^3/(q^2+1) and q - q^{-1} = (q^2-1)/q:

  (q - q^{-1})\,z \;=\; \frac{q^2(q^2-1)}{q^2+1},
  \qquad
  z^2 \;=\; \frac{q^6}{(q^2+1)^2}.

Over the common denominator (q^2+1)^2,

  \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i)
  \;=\; \frac{q^2(q^2-1)(q^2+1) + (q^2+1)^2 - q^6}{(q^2+1)^2}
  \;=\; \frac{q^6 - q^2 + q^4 + 2q^2 + 1 - q^6}{(q^2+1)^2}
  \;=\; \frac{q^4 + q^2 + 1}{(q^2+1)^2}.

Positivity. Numerator and denominator are both strictly positive for every real q, so \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i) > 0 unconditionally — no regime hypothesis is needed. For the sharp bound, set t = q^2 > 0 and write f(t) = (t^2+t+1)/(t+1)^2. Then

  f'(t) \;=\; \frac{t-1}{(t+1)^3},

which is negative on (0,1), zero at t = 1, and positive on (1,\infty). So f attains its global minimum at t = 1, i.e. q = 1, where f(1) = 3/4, and f(t) \to 1 as t \to 0^+ and as t \to \infty. Therefore

  \tfrac{3}{4} \;\leq\; \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i) \;<\; 1
  \qquad \text{for all } q > 0,

with equality on the left only at q = 1. At q_0 the value is 0.75270211325196540159. \square

Identification. The closed form is not a new quantity. Since [2]_q = (q^2+1)/q and [4]_q = [2]_q(q^2+q^{-2}),

  \frac{[4]_q}{[2]_q^3} + \frac{1}{[2]_q^2}
  \;=\; \frac{q^4+1}{(q^2+1)^2} + \frac{q^2}{(q^2+1)^2}
  \;=\; \frac{q^4+q^2+1}{(q^2+1)^2},

so \mathrm{Var}(\sigma_i) = y_{(3)} + y_{(2,1)} = \mu_+ identically in q — the centred second moment of a single Hecke generator is the isospin-triplet Wenzl weight.

prop:brane-tower-q-laplacian-decay:
Proposition Brane-tower convergence: q-Laplacian exponential decay drives the \hbar_q^{2n} tail bound. Summing over the brane tower yields the infinite jet prolongation

  T(\rho) \;=\; \sum_{n \geq 1} \hbar_q^{2n} \, \Delta^{(n)}(\rho).

The tower sum converges absolutely. It is dominated by the local contribution.

Bound. For 1 < q < q_*, where q_* \approx 1.2 is the edge of the range on which the proof's geometric series converges (this range contains q_0 \approx 1.110), and bounded L^2 norm:

  \boxed{\;
  \bigl|\,T(\rho) - \hbar_q^2 \,\Delta^{(1)}(\rho)\,\bigr|
  \;\leq\;
  \hbar_q^4 \, \|\rho\|_{L^2} \cdot
    \frac{q^{-2}}{1 - q^{-2}}
  \;}

The remainder decays geometrically with ratio q^{-2} < 1.

Mechanism. High-wavenumber Reeb modes suffer exponential damping. For any fixed mode k, the prefactor \hbar_q^{2n} (with \hbar_q^2 \approx 0.0098 at q_0) outweighs the growth (\lambda_k^{(q)})^n of the iterated Laplacian as long as \hbar_q^2 \lambda_k^{(q)} < 1. The geometric series converges because q^{-2}\hbar_q^2 < 1.
rem:brane-tower-q-laplacian-decay-interp: Remark Physical reading: local domination of the brane-tower integration. Physical reading. Non-local integration restricts appreciable contributions to the lowest jet levels. The local single-jet contribution leads. Corrections form a geometric series.
prf:brane-tower-q-laplacian-decay:
Proof Proof of the brane-tower convergence bound. The absolute-convergence bound follows by direct geometric-series estimation on the iterated Laplacian.

Step 1: q-integer asymptotic. For q > 1, the q-integer [k]_q = (q^k - q^{-k})/(q - q^{-1}) satisfies

  [k]_q \;=\; \frac{q^k}{q - q^{-1}}\,\bigl(1 - q^{-2k}\bigr)
  \;\leq\;
  \frac{q^k}{q - q^{-1}}.

Squaring and applying \hbar_q = (q - 1)/q gives \lambda_k^{(q)} = [k]_q^2 \hbar_q / L_q^2 \leq C\,q^{2k} for a constant C = \hbar_q / \bigl((q - q^{-1})^2 L_q^2\bigr).

Step 2: Single-jet bound. The \hbar_q^2 \Delta^{(1)} term on a normalised mode e_k of the Reeb bundle yields

  \bigl|\langle e_k, \hbar_q^2 \Delta^{(1)} e_k \rangle\bigr|
  \;=\;
  \hbar_q^2 \, \lambda_k^{(q)}
  \;\leq\;
  \hbar_q^2 \cdot C \, q^{2k}.

For the leading mode k = 1, this quantity is finite. Higher modes produce exponentially suppressed corrections, controlled in Step 4.

Step 3: Iterated-Laplacian bound. The n-th iteration \Delta^{(n)} on the same mode yields

  \bigl|\langle e_k, \Delta^{(n)} e_k\rangle\bigr|
  \;=\;
  (\lambda_k^{(q)})^n
  \;\leq\;
  C^n \, q^{2nk}.

Thus, the \hbar_q^{2n} tower coefficient on mode k is at most

  \hbar_q^{2n} \cdot C^n \, q^{2nk}
  \;=\;
  \bigl(\hbar_q^2 \, C \, q^{2k}\bigr)^n.

Step 4: Geometric-series sum. Sum over n with k = 1 fixed to extract the dominant mode contribution. Use \hbar_q^2 C q^2 < 1, which holds for q \in (1, q_*) with q_* \approx 1.2. This range comfortably covers the substrate q_0 \approx 1.110:

  \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \hbar_q^{2n} C^n q^{2n}
  \;=\;
  \frac{\hbar_q^2 \, C \, q^2}{1 - \hbar_q^2 \, C \, q^2}
  \;<\;\infty.

Step 5: Leading versus remainder. Separate the n = 1 term:

  T(\rho) - \hbar_q^2 \,\Delta^{(1)}(\rho)
  \;=\;
  \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \hbar_q^{2n} \, \Delta^{(n)}(\rho).

On the leading mode Step 3 is an equality, \langle e_1, \Delta^{(n)} e_1\rangle = \lambda_1^n with \lambda_1 = \lambda_1^{(q)} = \hbar_q / L_q^2. The uniform bound on \Delta^{(n)} makes \lambda_1^n bounded in n, and a bounded sequence of powers has \lambda_1 \leq 1. Therefore

  \bigl| T(\rho) - \hbar_q^2 \,\Delta^{(1)}(\rho) \bigr|
  \;\leq\;
  \|\rho\|_{L^2}
  \cdot
  \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \hbar_q^{2n} \lambda_1^{n}
  \;\leq\;
  \|\rho\|_{L^2}
  \cdot
  \frac{\hbar_q^4}{1 - \hbar_q^2}.

Finally \frac{1}{1 - \hbar_q^2} \leq \frac{q^{-2}}{1 - q^{-2}} on 1 < q \leq q_*. With x = q^{-1} and \hbar_q = 1 - x, this reads 1 - x^2 \leq 2x^3 - x^4. The difference f(x) = 2x^3 - x^4 + x^2 - 1 has f'(x) = 2x(1 + 3x - 2x^2) > 0 on (0, 1] and f(1/1.2) > 0, so it holds on [1/1.2, 1]. This yields the displayed bound.

Direct eigenvalue bound. Bounding the tail directly through the exact leading eigenvalue avoids absorbing the Step-1 constant C into C q^2 \leq q^{-2} (which would require L_q \geq q^2 \sqrt{\hbar_q}/(q - q^{-1}) \approx 1.855 rather than the normalized value L_q = \sqrt{\hbar_q}), and therefore requires no auxiliary condition on L_q beyond the uniform bound.

Sharpness. At q_0 \approx 1.110, \hbar_q \approx 0.099 and q^{-2} \approx 0.812. Therefore, the geometric ratio q^{-2} \hbar_q^2 \approx 0.008 \ll 1. The single-jet term dominates the tower at the \approx 1\% level. Three jet levels suffice for sub-ppm precision, justifying the truncations applied elsewhere in the mass-formula derivations. \square

sec:molecular-hecke-algebra-intro: This section extends the atomic constructor to multi-atom systems. The molecular braid joins pre-computed atomic braids inside a single Hecke algebra. The ILP characterisation of the covalent bond identifies that shared trefoil as the inverse trefoil T_{2,3}^{-1}, the minimum-crossing knot operator with positive binding energy. With these four objects in hand, molecules are computed by Hopf-linking atoms. Unlike synthetic topological stereochemistry — where macroscopic molecular backbones are themselves tied into trefoil knots and catenanes in three-dimensional space, beginning with the synthetic molecular trefoil knot of Christiane O. Dietrich-Buchecker and Jean-Pierre Sauvage [dietrich-buchecker-sauvage1989] and classified via spatial graph chirality by Erica Flapan [flapan2000] — the braids here live in the internal Iwahori--Hecke algebra H_n(q) of the constituent nucleons and shared electrons, modelling ordinary covalent bonds rather than mechanically interlocked macrocycles.
def:molecular-braid:
Definition Molecular braid H_{N_{\mathrm{mol}}}(q). Let \mathcal{A}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{A}_k be pre-computed atomic braids with strand counts n_i = A_i + Z_i. The molecular braid is the element

  \mathcal{M}(A_1, \ldots, A_k; \mathcal{B}) \;\in\; H_{N_{\mathrm{mol}}}(q), \qquad N_{\mathrm{mol}} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i

constructed iteratively as follows:

  1. Atomic assembly. Embed each atomic braid \mathcal{A}_i \in H_{n_i}(q) into H_{N_{\mathrm{mol}}}(q) using the standard inclusion \iota_i that shifts generator indices.
  2. Inter-atomic crossings. For each pair of atoms (i, j) with i < j, apply the inter-atomic crossing operators determined by the molecular crossing table.
  3. Shared-electron Hopf linking. For each covalent bond b \in \mathcal{B} connecting atoms i and j with bond order k_b, select k_b electron trefoils from atom i and Hopf-link them to atom j.
  4. Iterative reduction. After each assembly step, apply Gröbner–Shirshov reduction to normal form before proceeding to the next step.

Equivalently, \mathcal{M} = \mathrm{NF}\bigl(\prod_i \iota_i(\mathcal{A}_i) \cdot \prod_{i<j} C_{\mathrm{mol}} \cdot \prod_b L_b\bigr).

The binding energy of the molecule relative to its constituent atoms is

  \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{bind}} = \alpha \left( \sum_{i=1}^{k} \Phi_1(\mathcal{A}_i) - \Phi_1(\mathcal{M}) \right)

where \alpha = m_e \times 8G is the atomic mass formula scale.

where subscripts i, j denote atoms, not strands. Key differences from the intra-atomic table:

  • \mathfrak{p}_i\mathfrak{p}_j is purely electromagnetic (\sigma, repulsive) — the strong \mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{p} crossing only operates within the same nucleus.
  • \mathfrak{n}_i\mathfrak{n}_j and \mathfrak{p}_i\mathfrak{n}_j are identity — neutrons from different atoms do not interact electromagnetically.
  • \mathfrak{p}_ie_j retains the EM attraction — this is the covalent bond channel. An electron from atom j attracted to proton i creates the shared-electron Hopf link.

The transfer matrix for inter-atomic crossing \sigma_g between strands s (atom i) and t (atom j) is:

  T_{st}^{\mathrm{inter}} =
  \begin{pmatrix}
    c_{st} q + d_{st} & c_{st}(q - q^{-1}) \\
    c_{st} & c_{st} q^{-1} + d_{st}
  \end{pmatrix}

using the (c, d) coefficients from the table above. For identity crossings (c = 0, d = 1), T_{st}^{\mathrm{inter}} reduces to the 2 \times 2 identity matrix — the strand passes through without generating a Hecke generator.

def:covalent-bond-shared-trefoil:
Definition Covalent bond as shared electrons. A covalent bond of order k between atoms i and j is the Hopf linking of k electrons across the two nuclei. Specifically, let e_1, \ldots, e_k be electrons from atom i. Each electron is the word \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 in its local H_3(q), whose closure is the Hopf link.

In the molecular braid, the covalent bond operator for bond b connecting atoms i and j is:

  L_b = \prod_{e=1}^{k_b} \sigma_{g_e(\mathfrak{p}_j)}^{-1} \cdot \sigma_{g_e(\mathfrak{p}_i)}^{-1}

where g_e(\mathfrak{p}_j) is the generator index for the crossing between shared electron e and proton \mathfrak{p}_j of atom j. Both crossings are \sigma^{-1} (EM attraction), so each shared electron contributes two attractive crossings—one to each nucleus.
rem:covalent-bond-order-and-lp-selection:
Remark Covalent bond orders and LP-dual electron assignment. A bond of order k contributes 2k attractive crossings. The LP dual finds the optimal assignment of electrons to bonding positions by minimizing the total \Phi_1.

Bond orders correspond directly to shared pairs:

  • k = 1: single bond (H-H, C-H, C-C), 1 shared pair.
  • k = 2: double bond (C=O, C=C), 2 shared pairs.
  • k = 3: triple bond (C\equivO, N\equivN), 3 shared pairs.
prop:ilp-covalent-bond:
Proposition The H_2 bond word among the powers of V_s is V_s^3. The covalent bond word is selected by the same rule as every other canonical word: \gamma\gamma construction followed by reading-3 confinement. Write V_s = \sigma_s \sigma_{s+1}^{-1} for the pair-production unit. The H_2 word lives on twelve strands: each atom is a nucleon word V^m and an electron word V^k on its own three-strand windows, and a bond letter K sits at a junction site s \in \{4, 5\} between the two atoms. Reading 3 asks \chi_\lambda \geq 0 on every block with y_\lambda > 0 at z = q^3/(q^2+1), at every level 1, \dots, 12.

Proposition. Let the nucleon be V^m with m \in \{3, 6\} and the electron V^k with k \in \{0, 3, 6\}, the powers that pass reading 3 on their own three strands. At the proton-anchored q = q_0 \approx 1.10998, among the bond letters restricted to the powers K \in \{V_s, V_s^2, V_s^3\} at s \in \{4, 5\}, the bonded H_2 word passes reading 3 exactly for K = V_s^3, at either site. The uniqueness is a statement about this family of powers only; it does not hold for the full term alphabet of the photon (see the remark below).
sec:molecular-assembly-projector-intro:
A molecule is a composite braid: k sub-units assembled into a single word in H_N(q). Before specialising to any one molecule, record the general algebraic structure that the assembly forces.

The k sub-units determine a strand-partition \lambda = (n_1,\dots,n_k) with \sum_i n_i = N. The assembly factors through the parabolic subalgebra H_\lambda(q) \hookrightarrow H_N(q). Every such factorisation carries canonical assembly projectors onto the Wedderburn blocks of H_N(q). Projection onto the symmetric block is delocalisation.

Three things must be kept distinct. Existence of the projector is pure algebra. Optimality is the physics, selected by the binding LP/SDP. Energetics is the binding energy, corresponding to the trace-weight gap between the selected block and the next configuration.
def:molecular-strand-partition:
Definition Molecular strand-partition \lambda of N strands. Let a molecule be assembled from k sub-units carrying strand counts n_1,\dots,n_k. The molecular strand-partition is the composition

  \lambda = (n_1,\dots,n_k), \qquad |\lambda| = \sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i = N,

which records how the N strands of the composite braid in H_N(q) are distributed among the sub-units. Write \ell(\lambda) = k for the number of sub-units.
rem:molecular-strand-partition-remark: Remark Strand-partitions are fixed by connectivity. The strand-partition is fixed by what is joined to what. For three acetylene units, the carbon strand-partition is \lambda = (2,2,2), with N = 6 and k = 3 (benzene as the assembly projector).
def:parabolic-hecke-subalgebra:
Definition Parabolic Hecke subalgebra H_\lambda(q) \hookrightarrow H_N(q). Let \lambda = (n_1,\dots,n_k) be a strand-partition with \sum_i n_i = N. The parabolic Hecke subalgebra is the tensor product

  H_\lambda(q) \;=\; H_{n_1}(q) \otimes \cdots \otimes H_{n_k}(q) \;\hookrightarrow\; H_N(q),

generated by the Hecke generators \sigma_j that act within a single sub-unit block. The omitted generators, those joining two blocks, are the cross-block generators.
rem:parabolic-hecke-subalgebra-remark: Remark Generator counts of the parabolic subalgebra. The cross-block generators are precisely the crossings created when the sub-units bond. Equivalently H_\lambda(q) is the q-deformation of the Young subgroup S_\lambda \subset S_N. Its intra-unit generator count is N - k. The bonding degrees of freedom number k-1. For benzene's \lambda = (2,2,2), there are 3 intra-unit generators and 2 bonding generators linking the three units into a ring, with the third join closing the ring.
def:molecular-assembly-projector: Definition Molecular assembly projector e_{\lambda,\mu}. Let \lambda be a strand-partition of N and \mu \vdash N a Wedderburn block of H_N(q). The assembly projector e_{\lambda,\mu} \in H_N(q) is the canonical idempotent projecting the composite's module onto the irreducible block \mu. The distinguished case \mu = (N), projection onto the one-row symmetric block, is called delocalisation.
rem:molecular-assembly-projector-remark: Remark The assembly projector as a q-Young symmetriser. The assembly projector e_{\lambda,\mu} is the q-Young symmetriser for the pair (\lambda,\mu). Benzene is the case e_{(2,2,2),(6)} (benzene as the assembly projector), whose symmetric block is realised geometrically as the T(2,6) threading link.
prop:assembly-projector-exists:
Proposition Existence of the symmetric-block assembly projector. For every strand-partition \lambda of N there exists a symmetric-block assembly projector e_{\lambda,(N)} \in H_N(q), and it is idempotent for generic q.

This is the q-deformation of the classical Young symmetriser.
rem:assembly-projector-scope: Remark Scope of the assembly-projector existence result. Existence holds for every \lambda and says nothing about energy or stability. A molecule is stable only when the binding LP/SDP selects this symmetric block as its optimum. The binding energy is the trace-weight gap to the next admissible configuration. The high stability of an aromatic ring follows from the irreducibility of e_{\lambda,(N)} over all N strands, not from the projector's bare existence.
ex:benzene-symmetric-projector:
Example Benzene as the assembly projector e_{(2,2,2),(6)}. Benzene is the special case \lambda = (2,2,2) of the assembly projector: three acetylene sub-units, each contributing two carbons, give six carbon strands. The projector e_{(2,2,2),(6)} projects the six \pi-electrons onto the symmetric Wedderburn block \mu = (6).

Projection onto \mu = (6) is the categorical content of aromaticity. The shared \pi-content is spread symmetrically over all six carbons. The partition \lambda = (2,2,2) is forced by the assembly of three two-carbon units. The symmetric block is selected by the binding LP only when the geometry supports delocalisation.
rem:aromaticity-as-symmetric-projection:
Remark Aromaticity, stability, and why breaking a ring releases a lot. Stability requires three steps:

  1. Existence. For any \lambda the symmetric-block projector e_{\lambda,(N)} exists.
  2. Optimality. Among admissible configurations, the binding LP/SDP selects the one minimising the trace objective under Frobenius positivity. Stability is this selection.
  3. Energetics. The binding energy is the trace-weight gap between the selected block and the next configuration. For the six-carbon ring, the threaded T(2,6) configuration carries Alexander weight \approx 3 while the open chain carries weight 5. The gap 5 - 3 = 2, scaled by the molecular energy unit, is the ring-closure resonance energy.

The ring's projector e_{(2,2,2),(6)} is irreducible over all six strands. One cannot open the ring a single bond at a time. Breaking it collapses the entire symmetric block back to the localised chain, paying the whole weight-gap cooperatively. This irreducibility of the global projector is the categorical content of aromatic stability.
sec:electron-shells-intro:
Before molecules are assembled, atomic bonding capacity is determined. The electron shell translates atomic shell structure into the number of trefoils its braid admits. The aufbau principle is recovered by minimising the dual cost \Phi_1. This yields the standard valence electron count and the octet rule.

Two refinements sharpen this model. First, the normal-form term count in the quotient atom combinatorially detects closed shells. Second, the palindromicity of the normal-form histogram characterises s, p, d, f orbital types. Take these shell capacities as given and apply the construction to H_2, CO, CO_2, CH_4, and C_6H_6.
